coral-restoration.heroImageAlt: Oceans Alive community divers preparing for coral restoration at Kuruwitu
longDescription: Since 2019, Oceans Alive Foundation has partnered with Coral Guardian International and Coral Reef Care to build Kenya's most active community-led coral nursery at Kuruwitu. Local fishers - the same men and women whose livelihoods depend on the reef - are trained and employed as certified reef gardeners.

Coral fragments are grown in underwater nurseries attached to metal tree structures. Once colonies reach transplantable size, community divers carefully move them to bleached and degraded areas of the reef. The result: 24,800 coral colonies planted since 2019 with an 85% survival rate - well above the global average.

The programme is deliberately designed so that the community owns it. Fishers who once dynamite-fished now guard the same reef, because they have seen it come back to life with their own hands. Within the protected tengefu, fish biomass has increased by 400% - and the fish have started coming back outside it too.

bodyImages.alt: Two young Oceans Alive trained community divers
bodyImages.caption: Trained community divers - local fishers turned reef guardians

quote.text: The reef is not just recovering - it is growing. We see fish we have not seen in twenty years.
quote.author: Community diver, Kuruwitu

co-management.heroImageAlt: Community co-management meeting - Kilifi County, Kenya
longDescription: In January 2022, Oceans Alive Foundation made history: delivering Kenya's first formal ocean co-management plan under new government guidelines. The plan places 150 km² of sea - an area the size of a small city - under structured community stewardship, with Beach Management Units and local government sharing governance responsibility.

The LMMA (Locally Managed Marine Area) model is the culmination of nearly two decades of relationship-building between Oceans Alive, Kilifi County Government, the Kenya Ministry of Blue Economy, and the fishing communities who live at the heart of this work. What began with 30 hectares at Kuruwitu in 2003 is now a 120 km² internationally recognised governance blueprint.

Community co-management means that the people who fish the sea also write the rules about how it is fished. Rotational no-take zones, gear transition programmes, seasonal closures - all driven by community data, community decisions, and community enforcement. It's governance by the people it protects.

bodyImages.alt: Beach Management Unit meeting with community members
bodyImages.caption: A Beach Management Unit (BMU) meeting - community voices shaping marine policy

bodyImages.alt: Community members in a co-management planning circle
bodyImages.caption: Co-management planning sessions bring together fishers, elders and government officials

quote.text: When communities own their conservation, they defend it. When it provides livelihoods, they sustain it.
quote.author: Oceans Alive Foundation

project-reel.heroImageAlt: Project REEL Kilifi - Canon CENA documentation at Kuruwitu
longDescription: Project REEL Kilifi is a media partnership between Oceans Alive, Canon Central & North Africa (Canon CENA), and Athlete Media Group. The programme brings world-class photography and filmmaking to the Kilifi coast - documenting the conservation story and amplifying it to audiences that wouldn't otherwise hear it.

The visual documentation produced by Project REEL has appeared in international conservation media, supported OAF fundraising campaigns, and brought global attention to the Kuruwitu model. Photographs from the project have reached audiences across four continents.

Beyond storytelling, Project REEL trains local young people in photography and documentation - building a generation of Kenyan environmental communicators who can tell their own story in their own voice.

quote.text: Conservation that cannot be seen cannot inspire. Project REEL puts Kilifi on the world stage.
quote.author: Oceans Alive Foundation

uk-biodiversity.heroImageAlt: Capacity assessment workshop - UK Biodiversity Programme
longDescription: The UK Biodiversity Programme is an institutional capacity-building initiative funded by the UK Government through the FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office). It works to strengthen the organisational and governance infrastructure behind marine conservation in Kenya.

The programme focuses on the people and systems that make conservation work over the long term: training conservation managers, strengthening community governance structures, and building the policy frameworks that give community-led marine management legal standing.

Through this programme, Oceans Alive has deepened its engagement with national government bodies, supported the development of Kenya's marine governance framework, and built institutional capacity that extends well beyond any single project cycle.

ocean-education.heroImageAlt: Teacher showing coral to children at Kuruwitu - Ocean Education programme
longDescription: The tengefu - the protected space - is Oceans Alive's living classroom. Each year, more than 2,500 students, interns, and young people come to Kuruwitu to learn real marine conservation, not from textbooks, but from the reef itself.

Schools from across Kilifi County visit the sanctuary for guided learning days. Children snorkel above coral gardens, learn to identify reef species, and hear from community divers about what the reef looked like before - and what it looks like now. It's ocean literacy rooted in living evidence.

The internship programme brings aspiring conservationists from Kenya and around the world to train alongside OAF staff. They leave with practical skills in reef monitoring, community engagement, and marine governance - and many go on to build careers in conservation.

bodyImages.caption: The reef as a classroom - children discovering marine life at Kuruwitu

bodyImages.alt: Students in a learning session at the marine sanctuary
bodyImages.caption: Ocean literacy sessions at the Kuruwitu marine sanctuary

quote.text: When a child grows up protecting the ocean, it is protected for a generation. When they teach their children, it is protected forever.
quote.author: Ocean Education Programme

bmu-network.heroImageAlt: Beach Management Unit members in community meeting at Kilifi
longDescription: Beach Management Units (BMUs) are the legal bodies that represent fishing communities in Kenya's coastal governance system. Oceans Alive works to connect and strengthen the BMU network across Kilifi County - ensuring that fishers' voices carry real weight in decision-making at county and national level.

Through the Kilifi BMU Network, OAF facilitates regular inter-BMU coordination meetings, supports communities in documenting fishing pressure data, and provides training in fisheries management, legal rights, and governance processes.

The programme has contributed to a 400% increase in fish biomass within co-managed areas - evidence that when fishers govern their own waters, the ocean responds. The Kilifi BMU Network is now a model being examined by Kenya Fisheries Service for national rollout.

bodyImages.caption: Regular BMU coordination meetings keep community voices central to governance

bodyImages.alt: Fisherman on the Kilifi coast with fishing nets
bodyImages.caption: The fishers of Kilifi - the people the BMU Network exists to represent and empower

quote.text: When fishers govern their own waters, the ocean responds.
quote.author: Kilifi BMU Network

trash4cash.heroImageAlt: Women in Trash4Cash programme sorting plastic waste on the Kilifi coast
longDescription: Eight million tonnes of plastic enter the world's oceans every year. On the Kilifi coast, the women of the Trash4Cash programme are fighting back - and getting paid for it.

Trash4Cash brings together women's groups from coastal communities to collect, sort, and sell plastic waste to certified recyclers. What would otherwise end up in the ocean becomes household income. More than 80 women now participate across four communities, collecting over two tonnes of plastic waste every month.
By placing income generation and environmental protection in the same hands, Trash4Cash makes conservation something women do for their own futures, not something done to their environment.

turtle-protection.heroImageAlt: Community celebration of ocean conservation at Kilifi - World Ocean Day
longDescription: Sea turtles have swum Kenya's coastline for millions of years. Today, three species - the green turtle, hawksbill turtle, and loggerhead - nest along the Kilifi coast. All three are threatened.

Oceans Alive community rangers monitor nesting beaches year-round along 270 km of coastline, recording nesting events, tagging females, and protecting nests from poachers and disturbance. Data collected by the rangers feeds into Kenya's national turtle monitoring programme.

The programme is built on the understanding that communities who live alongside nesting turtles are the most effective guardians of those turtles. Community rangers are paid local people - often former poachers - who have chosen stewardship over exploitation because it supports their families and their identity.

quote.text: We watched the turtles almost disappear. Now we watch them come back. That is the greatest change of our lifetime.
quote.author: Community ranger, Kilifi coast

marine-governance.heroImageAlt: Marine policy documentation and governance work at Oceans Alive
longDescription: Conservation without policy is just gardening. Oceans Alive translates twenty years of community-collected data and field experience into national marine policy frameworks - ensuring that what works in Kilifi shapes how Kenya manages its entire 270 km coastline.

In 2022, OAF delivered Kenya's first ocean co-management plan under new government guidelines - a legal document placing 150 km² under community stewardship. In 2025, the Kuruwitu model was presented at the IUCN World Conservation Congress as a globally scalable blueprint for community-led marine governance.

The Marine Governance & Policy programme supports communities in generating the evidence that policymakers need, represents community interests at county and national government level, and advocates for legal frameworks that recognise community marine tenure across the Western Indian Ocean.

quote.text: From 30 hectares to a global blueprint. Community governance can scale.
quote.author: IUCN World Conservation Congress, 2025

kitchen-gardens.heroImageAlt: Coastal woman tending a kitchen garden - Kilifi County, Kenya
longDescription: On Kenya's coast, food security and ocean health are the same problem. When fish stocks decline, fishing families turn to more intensive harvesting - accelerating the collapse. Kitchen gardens break this cycle by providing alternative food sources and income, reducing pressure on the reef.

Oceans Alive's Kitchen Gardens & Food Security programme establishes climate-smart kitchen gardens for coastal fishing families across Kilifi County. Women who lead the gardens gain income from selling surplus produce, reducing their households' dependence on overexploited fish stocks.
The programme is intentionally integrated with Trash4Cash and the coral restoration work - because a community that has food security is a community that can afford to let the reef recover.

bodyImages.alt: Women laughing and holding fresh vegetables from kitchen gardens
bodyImages.caption: Kitchen garden produce - nutrition, income, and reduced pressure on the reef

quote.text: When the family has food from the garden, the father does not have to take every fish from the sea.
quote.author: Kitchen garden participant, Kilifi

capacity-building.heroImageAlt: Capacity assessment and training workshop - Oceans Alive Foundation
longDescription: Conservation only lasts as long as the people who carry it. Oceans Alive's Capacity Building & Training programme builds the human infrastructure that makes community-led marine conservation durable - beyond any single funder, project, or generation.

Training covers marine governance, protected area management, ecological monitoring, fisheries law, and community facilitation. Participants include BMU members, community rangers, women's group leaders, local government officials, and aspiring conservationists from across Kenya.

The programme deliberately trains people who will remain in the community after any given project ends - fishers, teachers, local leaders - because they are the ones who will carry the conservation work forward. International interns and students are also integrated into the programme, creating exchange that strengthens both local and global conservation capacity.

bodyImages.alt: Women in a capacity building training session with Oceans Alive
bodyImages.caption: Conservation training - building skills that last beyond any project cycle

community-health.heroImageAlt: Community gathering in Kilifi County - Oceans Alive health and wellbeing programme
longDescription: The health of Kilifi's coastal communities and the health of its ocean are inseparable. When fish stocks collapse, families go hungry. When plastic pollution rises, children get sick swimming in the sea. When livelihoods are insecure, mental health suffers.

Oceans Alive's Community Health & Wellbeing programme takes a holistic approach - linking ocean conservation directly to the physical, economic, and social wellbeing of the 1,200+ community members at the heart of its work.

The programme includes nutrition support through kitchen gardens, economic resilience through Trash4Cash, community health days linked to World Ocean Day celebrations, and partnerships with local health authorities on issues that intersect with environmental quality.

quote.text: A healthy ocean is a healthy community. We do not separate them.
quote.author: Oceans Alive Foundation

research-monitoring.heroImageAlt: Community reef monitoring divers - research and monitoring programme
longDescription: Good conservation is grounded in evidence. Oceans Alive's Research & Monitoring programme generates the ecological baselines, fish biomass surveys, coral cover assessments, and biodiversity data that underpin every other programme the organisation runs.

Community reef monitors - local trained divers - conduct regular transect surveys of the Kuruwitu tengefu and surrounding areas. Their data tracks coral cover recovery, fish biomass changes, and the expansion of species into previously degraded areas. This data is presented to Kenya Fisheries Service, county government, and international partners to inform marine policy.

At the IUCN World Conservation Congress in 2025, Oceans Alive presented a decade of reef monitoring data demonstrating that community-led marine governance produces measurable, sustained ecological recovery - making the Kilifi model the most evidence-backed community conservation programme in East Africa.

quote.text: Our data does not just tell us how the reef is doing. It tells the government how to protect it.
quote.author: Oceans Alive Research & Monitoring
